newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks closed thousands of pre-war accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks closed thousands of pre-war accounts.

text.p: Previously unpublished records seen by Reuters show that Swiss banks, already in trouble over the lost money of Jewish Holocaust victims, closed thousands of bank accounts without holders' knowledge after World War Two.

The records, recently uncovered in dusty Swiss cantonal archives in Lausanne, show the names of account holders and their savings now worth millions of dollars at current values which may open the way to fresh claims against Swiss banks.
Swiss banks, the world's most secretive, have repeatedly stated that they were missing many, if not all, of their old archives and documents.

But the records belonging to the Credit Foncier Vaudois Bank in Lausanne list thousands of people, mainly Swiss but including many foreigners, their bank account numbers, their towns and the time when they first deposited the money.
They included an Armenian named Charles Doctorian who had opened an account in 1931 worth $70,000 at today's value, and one Octave Weber with an account dating from 1932 worth nearly $10,000 today.
Edward Fagan, one of the main lawyers in a $20 billion U.S. lawsuit filed against Swiss banks by the heirs of Holocaust victims, said the lists would provide a roadmap to where the money had gone.
"These lists are very significant," he told Reuters by telephone from New York. "I'm pleased to see all the things my clients have been saying are true, that there are documents."
Until recently, Swiss banks had to keep documents going back 10 years.
But under laws passed in 1995 under international criticism, the banks are not allowed to destroy any documents that could relate to the search for the missing money of Holocaust victims.
During the growing controversy, it has never been clear where the money from the dormant accounts went.
Swiss banks, after a year of arguing with Jewish groups, acknowledged in February that they held 39 million Swiss francs in ownerless accounts that might stem from Holocaust victims.
But the World Jewish Congress (WJC) rejected the sum as too small, saying there may be billions of dollars more.
Spokeswoman Silvia Matile of the Swiss Bankers Association, told Reuters the account closures were "regrettable."

Matile said banks before 1995 could publish in the official cantonal gazette that they wanted to close an account. If the client did not come, then they could close the account and destroy any files after keeping them for 10 years.
The money from closed accounts was often sent to charities.
"Now, it's forbidden for banks to use such procedures," Matile said. "But we have to see the times as they were then, when we didn't know what would be happening today."
It appears the banks made little effort to find the owners of accounts being slated for closure.

"We tried to find the people. But it depends on the volume. We can't make a big investigation abroad only for 200 francs," said Bernard Kraehenbuehl, a senior director at the Lausanne-based Banque Cantonal Vaudoise, Switzerland's fifth biggest bank which took over the Credit Foncier Vaudoise Bank.

Jean Ziegler, a Socialist member of the Swiss parliament and an outspoken critic of the government's and banks' handling of the crisis, said the accounts and names in the Lausanne archives probably represented just a tiny fraction of the total.
"This is just the tip of an iceberg," he said. "This is only the beginning."

"Swiss banks are saying they've lost the money, but there is no such thing as lost money in Swiss banks. Swiss bankers are absurdly precise book-keepers. This is one of the Swiss virtues. They cheat and lie to their clients and to the world, but they are book-keepers by heart."
